criteria.note: The TL;DR block sits at the very top and answers 'can a celiac travel Korea, and how' within the first ~200 words, immediately followed by a celiac-specific rules section.

Title is 35 chars (55 with the appended ' | Gluten-Free Korea'), description is 146 chars, the keyword 'celiac travel korea' is present in both, and the description lists distinct content rather than restating the title.

Headings like 'What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works', and the Tier 1/2/3 split carry the argument on a skim rather than merely labelling sections.
Well over three contextually earned links (restaurants roundup, bakeries post, phrases guide, BBQ guide, label guide, snacks post), each placed where a reader would naturally want more depth.
All five frontmatter Q/As are established in the body (BBQ script, tamari caveat, 237 Pizza status, 10% wheat bakery) and each answer stands alone as a rich result.

Dated, specific, and includes failures: a summer 2026 closed-for-remodelling visit, a summer 2025 franchise call, a product quietly renamed from 'gluten-free bread' to 'rice bread', and pink-vs-green packets of the same snack brand.

Korean terms are given with hangul and romanisation (간장 ganjang, 밀떡 mil-tteok, 뻥튀기 ppeongttwigi), and named products and ratios (Goraesa, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, '90% rice flour, 10% wheat flour') are checkable.

Primary sources are linked with retrieval or publication dates — the MFDS 식품등의 표시기준 ('text in force as of August 2026'), Orion's own product page ('re-verified August 2026'), and the blogger roundup ('published October 2023').

The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish ('our standard is NCGS, and we can't audit a kitchen'), retracts an unverifiable GFCO claim, and carries no commercial or affiliate links requiring disclosure.

findings.quote: *Updated August 2026: added the MFDS labeling-standard and manufacturer citations, dated our franchise call, removed a certification claim we could no longer verify, corrected the tteokbokki entry to cover 밀떡 (wheat tteok), and flagged 237 Pizza as unconfirmed — it was closed for remodelling on our last visit. The August 2026 retrieval dates below are from that update.*
findings.why: A 60-word editorial changelog is the first thing above the TL;DR, spending prime above-the-fold space on maintenance metadata rather than on the traveler's question. It does not break intent-match, but it delays it for a reader who lands from search.
findings.fix: Move the changelog to the footer next to the existing 'First published April 2026 · last updated August 2026' line, leaving a one-line 'Updated August 2026' stamp at the top if freshness signalling is wanted.

findings.quote: 1. **If you're celiac, start here** — the five stricter rules, up front
findings.why: The 'In This Guide' table of contents is plain bolded text rather than anchor links, so on a long page it describes the structure without letting a reader jump to the section they came for.
findings.fix: Convert each TOC entry to an in-page anchor link matching the corresponding heading id.

findings.quote: The non-Orion entries trace to a Korean blogger's roundup ([seiming.tistory.com](https://seiming.tistory.com/243), published October 2023), so treat them as leads
findings.why: The provenance is disclosed and dated, which is why no point is withheld, but a 2023 personal-blog roundup is the weakest link in an otherwise primary-sourced article, and snack formulations change faster than that.
findings.fix: Replace the Doritos, Banana Kick, and Yegam entries with links to the manufacturers' own product pages (Lotte, Nongshim, Orion) carrying their own retrieval dates, and keep the blogger link only as a secondary 'where we first heard this' note.

criteria.note: Nearly everything is either sourced (MFDS notice, Orion product page, dated franchise call, dated blogger roundup) or explicitly framed as the couple's own field observation, but the 237 Pizza owner's medical history and the 'only one in Korea' superlative are asserted flat with no source and no observation marker.
criteria.evidence_quote: A fully gluten-free pizzeria — to our knowledge the only one in Korea. The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research

criteria.note: Product names (Poca Chip Original vs Onion, Yegam, Banana Kick, Chamsal Seolbyeong, Goraesa), the Orion page, the tistory post date, the summer-2025 call, and the April/August 2026 publication dates are all checkable and internally consistent with each other and with the frontmatter date.

The piece states exactly how it knows each class of claim — visits, kitchen conversations, a dated phone call, a manufacturer page, a blogger roundup treated as 'leads' — and names what those methods cannot establish ('we can't audit a kitchen', 'field notes, not a database').

NCGS is separated from celiac in the standfirst, a dedicated up-front celiac section, the tier headers and individual entries; shared grills, shared fryers, shared kitchens and shared-facility disclaimers are all named; no entry is given an unqualified safety guarantee.
Every time-sensitive source carries a retrieval or occurrence date and the elapsed time is stated where it bites ('A year has passed since that call'), plus a standing reformulation caution.

The load-bearing fact is correct and stated twice — mandatory allergen labelling flags wheat only, with 보리 and 호밀 excluded — and 밀/소맥/소맥분, 밀떡 vs 쌀떡, 원재료명, 집간장 and the phrase scripts are all used correctly.

The reader is handed the law text, the manufacturer's own allergen page, the exact hangul strings to scan, the reconfirmation script, and an explicit instruction that the packet in hand overrides the article.

findings.quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research — partly out of frustration that no one else in Korea had.
findings.why: This is third-party medical information and a market superlative presented as established fact, with neither a source nor the 'this is what we were told' marker the article uses elsewhere. It does not by itself drive an eating decision, but it lends the venue credibility a reader may weigh.
findings.fix: Attribute it: 'The owner told us he has celiac disease himself' — and either cite or soften the 'no one else in Korea had' framing to match the existing 'to our knowledge' hedge.

findings.quote: a dedicated operation removes the shared-fryer and flour-dust problem by design
findings.why: 'Removes ... by design' is stronger than the evidence the article itself admits to ('we can't audit a kitchen'). Dedicated facilities still carry supplier-ingredient and delivery-side gluten risk. The surrounding sentences do carry the caveat, so this is not blocking, but the verb is doing more work than the method supports.
findings.fix: Change to 'is designed to remove' or 'removes by design, in principle — we have not verified sourcing or supply chain', keeping the existing counter-question advice.

findings.quote: He also sells travel-sized packets of gluten-free gochujang and gluten-free soy sauce, which you can throw in a bag before a Korean BBQ night.
findings.why: The article's own thesis is that a 'gluten-free' label in Korea often means low-gluten until proven otherwise, yet these two products are described with the label taken at face value and no instruction to check the 원재료명 — an inconsistency a celiac reader could act on.
findings.fix: Apply the article's own rule: note whether you read the ingredient list on these packets, and tell readers to check them like any other product.
